turns.content: The Hartree energy is defined by 1 E_h = m_e e^4/(16 pi^2 epsilon_0^2 hbar^2), where m_e is the electron mass, e the elementary charge, epsilon_0 the vacuum permittivity, and hbar the reduced Planck constant. Using standard SI values, evaluate 1 E_h in joules.
Starting from the definition of an electron volt as the energy gained by one elementary charge across a potential difference of 1 volt, express 1 eV in joules using e = 1.6022 x 10^-19 C.

Before doing the numerical conversion, identify the dimensionless ratio that converts an energy in joules to electron volts. Using 1 eV = 1.6022 x 10^-19 J, should one Hartree correspond to more or less than one electron volt?
Substitute your joule values for 1 E_h and 1 eV into the chemical equilibrium constant for 1 E_h in electron volts. Write the expression without rounding the quotient.
Evaluate the quotient with the available digits and compare the size of one Hartree with one electron volt.
Round the converted value to five significant figures and state how the significant figures in the constants limit the precision.
Cross-check the energy independently from E_h = e^2/(4 pi epsilon_0 a_0), using a_0 = 5.2918 x 10^-11 m, and confirm that it is consistent with the joule value used above.

Using the result of the cross-check, report the final value of 1 E_h in electron volts, show the joule-to-electron-volt quotient, and state whether one Hartree is larger or smaller than one electron volt.
